summary: Stone dwelling with an octagonal birdcage-lantern tower at the mouth of the Salmon River on Lake Ontario, lit 1838, dark from 1859, a hotel in the 20th century and a rental today.

lens.note: Sixth-order Fresnel lens (270 degrees) installed during Charles M. Lewis's service; before that, eight lamps with 14-inch reflectors

structures.type: octagonal tower on a stone dwelling
structures.note: Contract called for a stone dwelling 25 by 30 ft and an octagonal tower 16 ft above the walls; USLHS record gives wood tower on a fieldstone house

access.note: Privately owned. Grounds open; dwelling and tower open to overnight guests (LighthouseFriends). Sited at the Salmon River Lighthouse & Marina.

stay.note: Vacation rental: three bedrooms, up to eight guests (LighthouseFriends); the Society's listing offers the 1st floor, the 2nd floor, or both.

facts.agency: Private: a corporation formed by a group of individuals to buy the property in 1987 (Salmon River Lighthouse & Marina); new owners since 2014 per LighthouseFriends

events.note: Congress appropriates $3,000 for the lighthouse, 3 March 1837
Land purchased at the river mouth, 1 September 1837
Stone dwelling with octagonal tower completed; total cost $2,999.94
Exhibited for the first time in August 1838 by keeper Lewis Conant
Sixth-order Fresnel lens (270 degrees) with a single Hains mineral-oil fountain lamp, during Lewis's service (1854-1857)
Sold at public auction to Leopold Joh for $155 on 16 October 1895
Hotel complex developed around the lighthouse
Hotel sold to a family that enlarged it
Property bought by a group that formed a corporation
Coast Guard-approved solar light in the lantern; reactivated 6 August 1989 as a Class II aid, Port Ontario Light
New owners took over the property

corrections.proposed: stone dwelling with a wood octagonal tower (the USLHS record and Wikipedia give wood tower on fieldstone house)
corrections.why: The USLHS record says 'WOOD TOWER ON FIELDSTONE HOUSE'; the 1837 specification asks for a stone dwelling and an octagonal tower, without naming the tower's material. Check the NRHP nomination before editing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and USLHS: 1859. Wikipedia's infobox and keeper list: 1858. The story uses 1859 and notes the difference.
USLHS and LighthouseFriends give Weed to 1859; Wikipedia gives March 1857 to 1858.

notes_for_editor: Thin primary evidence. The NRHP nomination (79001618) is not digitised at NPGallery (placeholder), and the corpus holds no Lighthouse Board report before 1891, so the 1837-1859 details come from LighthouseFriends, which quotes the Lighthouse Board and Lt. Platt. Those quotations are second-hand and the story says so. Newspaper search (Chronicling America, New York 1838-1880) returned no relevant page. Wikipedia is leads-only and is not cited; its keeper and deactivation dates differ (see resolved_conflicts), and it says the former hotel was razed in early 2016, which is not verified here. The keeper roster is four lines from USLHS. The hotel-era owners are named only as families and the corporation; the 1987 group and the 2014 owners are not named. The record's 'stone' tower material is doubtful (USLHS: wood tower on fieldstone house). The NRHP listing date (1979) and the 'Fl W 2s' characteristic are not verified from a source read. The brief dates this batch 2026-10-22; the system date was 2026-10-27, which is the accessed date used. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the USLHS accommodations page prints 'Breakfast is cooked by the resident Keeper' and the half-mile trail sentence under its Saugerties Lighthouse entry, not Selkirk. Both were removed from the story and the JSON; nothing in the Selkirk entry supports a resident keeper or a walking route. The draft called Lt. Platt a 'lighthouse inspector'; LighthouseFriends says only that Lieutenant Platt stopped by and reported, so the word is removed. The bid-notice wording 'extend sixteen feet above the walls' is LighthouseFriends' own narrative of the notice, not a quotation from it; the story now says so.
